Yes — **order can change** in `ml.json` (and every other locale). That is not the real problem.

A Malayalam translator can already write:

```json
"greet_user": "<2>{{user}} 👋</2> <1>Good {{time_of_day}},</1>"
```

`<1>` / `<2>` and `{{user}}` / `{{time_of_day}}` can move anywhere. Crowdin translators edit those files; `en.json` is only the source string.

**What they cannot fix** is that the English sentence is built from leftover parts:

```
"Good" + t("morning")  →  "Good Morning, Yaswanth 👋"
```

`t("morning")` is the word *Morning*, not a greeting. Many languages do not work that way.

| Language | Natural greeting | Not this |
|---|---|---|
| Malayalam | സുപ്രഭാതം | നല്ല + രാവിലെ |
| Hindi | शुभ प्रभात | अच्छा + सुबह |
| German | Guten Morgen | Gut + Morgen |
| Spanish | Buenos días | Bueno + mañana |

"Good" even changes shape (Guten / Buenos). A translator stuck with `"Good {{time_of_day}}"` has to fake a sentence around an English-shaped slot. Dropping `"Good"` and keeping `{{time_of_day}}` still leaves that slot.

---

**Three full greeting strings is the right fix.** Give translators a complete sentence and only interpolate the name:

```json
"greet_user_morning": "<1>Good morning,</1> <2>{{user}} 👋</2>",
"greet_user_afternoon": "<1>Good afternoon,</1> <2>{{user}} 👋</2>",
"greet_user_evening": "<1>Good evening,</1> <2>{{user}} 👋</2>"
```

Then pick which key in code, instead of stitching words:

```tsx
const period = hour < 12 ? "morning" : hour < 18 ? "afternoon" : "evening";

<Trans
  i18nKey={`greet_user_${period}`}
  values={{ user: formatName(user) }}
  components={{
    1: <span />,
    2: <span className="font-semibold text-gray-950" />,
  }}
/>
```

Malayalam can then be a real greeting, name wherever it belongs:

```json
"greet_user_morning": "<1>സുപ്രഭാതം,</1> <2>{{user}} 👋</2>"
```

Keep using `morning` / `afternoon` / `evening` for labels like slot names. Those are nouns, not greetings.

**Takeaway:** reordering tags is already allowed. The review comment is right — stop composing `"Good" + time-of-day`. Use three full strings. That is the usual i18n rule: never concatenate sentence fragments.

content.text:
Fixed. The greeting is now three complete sentences, and the code picks among them with a helper that returns **full key literals** — not a template string.

`greetUserKey()` returns `"greet_user_morning"`, `"greet_user_afternoon"`, or `"greet_user_evening"` as whole strings. Search, unused-key cleanup, and i18n tooling can see each key in source. `` `greet_user_${period}` `` hides those names, so scanners and grep miss them.

That is the usual i18n rule: never build key names at runtime. i18next `context` would keep `i18nKey="greet_user"` static, but then `greet_user_morning` would exist only in JSON and look unused. Literal returns avoid that.

English source is now:

```json
"greet_user_afternoon": "<1>Good afternoon,</1> <2>{{user}} 👋</2>",
"greet_user_evening": "<1>Good evening,</1> <2>{{user}} 👋</2>",
"greet_user_morning": "<1>Good morning,</1> <2>{{user}} 👋</2>"
```

Malayalam can be a real greeting (`സുപ്രഭാതം, {{user}}`) with the name wherever it belongs. Other locale files are left to Crowdin.

`morning` / `afternoon` / `evening` stay as generic labels; they are no longer glued into the greeting.
